As the world continues to navigate the challenges posed by COVID-19, various tips and home remedies have circulated widely on social media. One such claim, “Drinking hot water every 15 min helps fighting COVID-19,” has gained significant attention and prompted debate among users seeking simple ways to protect themselves from the virus. This article aims to examine the validity of this claim by analyzing its scientific basis and providing context around COVID-19 prevention.

COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which primarily spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. The virus can also spread by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching the mouth, nose, or eyes. Since the beginning of the pandemic, public health agencies have emphasized established preventive measures such as vaccination, hand hygiene, wearing masks, and maintaining physical distance.

The suggestion to drink hot water every 15 minutes is rooted in the belief that frequent consumption of heated liquids can flush the virus from the throat down into the stomach, where it will be destroyed by stomach acid. This idea has been widely shared online and through messaging apps, often accompanied by advice from purported medical professionals. However, upon closer examination, there is no scientific evidence supporting the effectiveness of this practice against COVID-19.

Firstly, the virus infects the respiratory tract, including the nose, throat, and lungs. It does not reside exclusively in the throat, and drinking water—hot or cold—does not "wash" the virus away or prevent infection. Once the virus has entered the body, it rapidly attaches to cells in the mucous membranes of the respiratory tract, which are not accessible to ingested liquids. Moreover, the virus can begin multiplying before causing symptoms, and by the time symptoms appear, it may have already spread within the body.

Secondly, while staying hydrated is important for overall health and can support the body’s immune system, the temperature or frequency of water consumption does not impact the likelihood of contracting COVID-19 or its progression. The human body maintains a stable internal temperature, and drinking hot water will not alter conditions in the throat or respiratory tract to a degree that would neutralize the virus.

Medical experts and public health organizations have repeatedly clarified that there are no shortcuts or home remedies that can prevent or cure COVID-19. The best ways to reduce the risk of infection include vaccination, proper mask usage, frequent handwashing, and avoiding close contact with individuals who may be infected.

In summary, the claim that “Drinking hot water every 15 min helps fighting COVID-19” is not supported by scientific evidence. While hydration is beneficial for health, it is not a preventive measure or cure for COVID-19. Individuals are advised to follow guidance from reputable health authorities and rely on proven methods to protect themselves and others from the virus. Misinformation, even when well-intentioned, can undermine public health efforts and should be approached with caution.

Selle artikli eesmärk on uurida seda väidet, analüüsides selle teaduslikku põhjendatust ja andma konteksti koronaviruse ennetamise kohta.

Koronaviruse, SARS-CoV-2, põhjustatud haigus levib peamiselt hingamisruumi lilledes, kui infektsioonilise inimese hooneb, hingab või kõhutab. Virus võib ka levida käsitsi kinnitatud pinnadest, siis kui inimene kõrvale kätt, nägu või silmad. Kui virus on juba kehas, ühendub see kiiresti hingamisruumi mukusmembraanide kudedega, mis ei ole saavutatavad ingestiooniga vedelike kaudu. Samuti võib virus alustada kahjustust enne sümptomeid, ja kui sümptomid ilmnevad, võib see juba levinud kehas.

Teiseks, kui vea tarbimine on oluline tervislikuks eluks ja toetab keha immuunsüsteemi, siis vee temperatuur või sagedus ei mõjuta koronaviruse levimise või arengu tõenäosust. Inimkeha hoiab enda temperatuuri stabiilseks, ja soojade vee tarbimine ei muuda hõbepõhja või hingamisruumi olulisi tingimusi nii, et viruse neutraliseerimiseks oleks piisavalt mõju.

Tervishoiuteadlased ja avalikud tervishoiuorganisatsioonid on korduvalt selgitanud, et pole lühikese sammuga või kodutööd, mis aitaks ennetada või ravida koronaviruse. Parimad viisid infektsiooni riski vähendamiseks on vaktsineerimine, korrektselt maski kasutamine, sagedane käte puhastamine ja hoida kaugust kahjustatud inimestega.

Kokkuvõttes, väide, et "soojade veega iga 15 minutit juua aitab võidelda koronavirusega", ei toeta teaduslikke tõendeid. Kui vee tarbimine on tervislik, siis see pole ennetusviis või ravim koronaviruse eest. Inimestel on soovitatav järgida usaldusväärsi tervishoiuorganisatsioonide soovitusi ja puhastada oma ja teiste tervist tõhusate meetoditega. Väärteadlik infot, isegi kui see on tugevdav, võib kahjustada avaliku tervishoiu tööd ja tuleb hoolikalt haldada.

In recent months, social media platforms have seen a resurgence of claims asserting that there has been no increase in mortality rates across Europe during the COVID-19 pandemic, suggesting that concerns about the virus and its impact are exaggerated. This narrative has gained traction among groups skeptical of public health measures or the severity of the disease. To assess the accuracy of these assertions, it is essential to examine the available data and understand the broader context surrounding mortality statistics during the pandemic.

Mortality rates are commonly used as a key indicator of public health, and during extraordinary events such as pandemics, statisticians and health authorities monitor "excess mortality." Excess mortality refers to the number of deaths above what would be expected based on historical averages for a given period. This method accounts for seasonal fluctuations and long-term trends, providing a clearer picture of the impact of significant events, including pandemics.

When COVID-19 emerged in early 2020, European countries began reporting weekly and monthly mortality data, allowing for real-time analysis of its effects. Throughout 2020 and 2021, most European nations experienced a marked increase in deaths compared to previous years. For instance, countries such as Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany saw notable spikes in excess mortality, particularly during the initial waves of the pandemic and subsequent surges.

This increase was not uniform across all regions or time periods, as factors such as public health interventions, vaccination rollouts, and local outbreaks influenced mortality numbers. However, the general trend was clear: Europe saw periods where deaths far exceeded typical levels. These surges correlated with spikes in COVID-19 cases, hospitalizations, and strain on healthcare systems, further underscoring the connection between the pandemic and increased mortality.

It is also important to consider that COVID-19-related deaths are not always immediately distinguishable from other causes, due to complications such as underreporting, misclassification, and indirect effects—such as delays in medical treatment for non-COVID conditions during lockdowns and high hospital occupancy. Nevertheless, the overall excess mortality figures capture the cumulative impact of the pandemic, both directly and indirectly.

Some social media users point to more recent data, suggesting that mortality rates have returned to pre-pandemic levels, and thus concluding that concerns about COVID-19 were unfounded. While it is true that after the widespread availability of vaccines and improved treatment protocols, deaths in many European countries have approached normal levels, this does not negate the significant mortality increases observed during the height of the pandemic.

In summary, the claim that there was no mortality increase in Europe during the COVID-19 pandemic is not supported by the evidence. Data from multiple European countries reveal distinct periods of excess deaths corresponding with COVID-19 outbreaks. Although mortality rates have stabilized more recently, the impact of the pandemic in terms of increased deaths was both real and substantial, reflecting the gravity of the crisis faced by Europe and the world.

Həqiqətən də, vaksinlərin təqdim edilməsi və sağlamlıq təşkili proseslərinin yaxşılaşması nəticəsində Avropa ölkələrində ölümlər normallıq səviyyəsinə yaxınlaşmışdır. Avropa ölkələrinin məlumatları pandemiyalı dövrlərdə aşırı ölümlər nəzərə alınan dövrləri göstərir. Hələ də ölümlər daha sonraki dövrlərdə sabitləşmişdir, lakin pandemiyalı dövrdə ölümlərin artması həqiqətən və əhəmiyyətli oldu, bu da Avropa və dünya üçün təqdir edilə biləcək bir kriz kimi görünür.

A recent Facebook post claims that coronavirus infections were successfully treated in Moscow 40 years ago using Arbidol and other pills, suggesting that the notion of there being no medication for coronavirus is a falsehood. This claim has attracted attention amid ongoing debates about treatments for COVID-19 and other coronaviruses. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is important to examine the history of coronaviruses, the development and use of Arbidol, and the context surrounding antiviral treatments.

Coronaviruses are a family of viruses that can cause illnesses ranging from the common cold to more severe diseases such as SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome), MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome), and COVID-19, which emerged in late 2019. While milder forms of coronavirus have circulated among humans for decades, the novel coronavirus that causes COVID-19 is distinct from those earlier strains.

Arbidol, also known as umifenovir, is an antiviral medication developed in Russia in the late 1980s and approved for use in Russia and China for the prevention and treatment of influenza and other respiratory viral infections. While Arbidol is a well-known medicine in Russia, it was not developed or widely used as early as 40 years ago, as the post claims. Furthermore, its use has largely been limited to influenza and not specifically for coronaviruses.

The claim that coronavirus was “successfully treated in Moscow 40 years ago with Arbidol and other pills” is problematic for several reasons. Firstly, the term “coronavirus” encompasses a variety of viruses. The most notable and severe outbreaks—such as SARS, MERS, and COVID-19—emerged only in the 21st century. Prior to the SARS outbreak in 2002-2003, coronaviruses were generally associated with mild symptoms similar to the common cold, and there is no evidence of a major coronavirus epidemic in Moscow or anywhere else around 40 years ago.

Secondly, Arbidol’s antiviral properties have been the subject of ongoing research, but its efficacy against the novel coronavirus responsible for COVID-19 remains unproven by large, high-quality clinical trials recognized by the global scientific community. While some laboratory studies suggest potential antiviral effects, the World Health Organization and most Western regulatory agencies have not authorized Arbidol as a treatment for COVID-19 due to insufficient evidence.

Finally, the assertion that “the idea that there is no medication is a lie” oversimplifies the nature of medical treatment for viral diseases. While there are antiviral drugs for certain viruses, until recently there was no universally accepted, highly effective medication for treating COVID-19. Treatment approaches have evolved rapidly as more evidence has become available.

In summary, the social media post misrepresents the history and treatment of coronaviruses. There is no record of successful treatment of a significant coronavirus outbreak in Moscow 40 years ago with Arbidol, as the drug was not developed until later and was not designed specifically for coronaviruses. Additionally, its effectiveness against COVID-19 has not been conclusively demonstrated. The claim that medications for coronavirus have long existed is therefore misleading and not supported by historical or scientific evidence.

"கொரோனா வைரஸ் மாஸ்கோவில் 40 ஆண்டுகளுக்கு முன்பு ஆர்பிடில் மற்றும் மற்ற மாதிரிகள் மூலம் வெற்றிகரமாக குணப்படுத்தப்பட்டது" என்ற வாதம் பல காரணங்களுக்காக மிகவும் தவறானது. முதலாவதாக, "கொரோனா வைரஸ்" என்பது பல வைரஸ்களைக் குறிக்கிறது. மிகவும் முக்கியமான மற்றும் மோசமான வைரல் வெளிப்பாடுகள், உதாரணமாக SARS, MERS மற்றும் COVID-19 என்பது 21-ம் நூற்றாண்டில் தான் உருவானது. SARS வெளிப்பாடு 2002-2003 ஆண்டுகளில் காணப்பட்டது, அதற்கு முன்பு கொரோனா வைரஸ்கள் சில சமயங்களில் சளி போன்ற சிறிய குறைந்த தொற்றுகளை ஏற்படுத்தும் வகையில் பரவியது. 40 ஆண்டுகளுக்கு முன்பு மாஸ்கோ அல்லது வேறு எங்கும் முக்கியமான கொரோனா வைரஸ் தொற்று இருந்தது என்ற தகவல் இல்லை.

இரண்டாவதாக, ஆர்பிடிலின் எதிர்வைரஸ் பண்புகள் தொடர்ந்து ஆராயப்பட்டு வருகின்றன, ஆனால் அது கொரோனாவை ஏற்படுத்தும் கொரோனாவின் தற்போதைய வைரஸுக்கு எதிராக பரிசோதனைகளின் விளைவாக கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்தும் மருந்தாக அங்கு இல்லை. இது மிகவும் பெரிய பரிசோதனைகள் மற்றும் உலக சுகாதார நிறுவனம் மற்றும் மிகவும் முக்கியமான கிழக்கு நிர்வாகங்கள் கொண்டு கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்தும் மருந்தாக அங்கு இல்லை. மேலும் சில செய்திகள் எதிர்வைரஸ் விளைவுகளை காட்டுகின்றன, ஆனால் அது கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்தும் மருநதாக அங்கு இல்லை என்று அறிவிக்கிறது.

இறுதியாக, "கொரோனாவிற்கு மருந்து இல்லை என்ற கருத்து தவறானது" என்ற வாதம் வைரல் நோய்களுக்கான மருத்துவ குணப்படுத்தும் முறைகளின் வகைகளை சுருக்கமாகக் கூறுகிறது. சில வைரஸ்களுக்காக எதிர்வைரஸ் மருந்துகள் உள்ளன, ஆனால் கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்தும் மருந்துகளுக்கு கடந்த காலமாக உலக முழுமையாக பெரிய விளைவுகளைக் கொண்ட மருந்து இல்லை. மேலும் சமீபத்திய விளைவுகள் கிடைத்துள்ள போது குணப்படுத்தும் முறைகள் விரைவாக மாறிவருகின்றன.

மொத்தமாக, சமூக வலைதள பதிவு கொரோனா வைரஸின் வரலாறு மற்றும் குணப்படுத்தும் முறைகளை தவறாக விளக்குகிறது. 40 ஆண்டுகளுக்கு முன்பு மாஸ்கோவில் ஆர்பிடில் மூலம் முக்கியமான கொரோனா வைரஸ் தொற்றை வெற்றிகரமாக குணப்படுத்தியது என்ற தகவல் இல்லை, ஏனெனில் அந்த மருந்து கடந்த காலமாக மட்டுமே மேம்படுத்தப்பட்டது மற்றும் கொரோனாவை ஏற்படுத்தும் வைரஸ்களுக்கு குறிப்பாக உருவாக்கப்படவில்லை. இதன் கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்தும் விளைவுகள் சரியாக காட்டப்படவில்லை. கொரோனாவிற்கு மருந்துகள் நீண்ட காலமாக இருந்தது என்ற வாதம் தவறானது மற்றும் வரலாற்று அல்லது அறிவியல் ஆதாரங்களுக்கு அதிரடி கொடுக்கவில்லை.
article_summary: Социальные сети распространили утверждение о лечении коронавируса в Москве 40 лет назад с помощью Арбидола, но это не соответствует историческим и научным данным. Арбидол был разработан в 1980-х и не использовался для коронавирусов, а крупные вспышки таких вирусов, как СARS и МЕRS, начали происходить только в 21-м веке. Эффективность Арбидола против нового коронавируса (СОВИД-19) не подтверждена клиническими исследованиями, что делает заявления о существовании лекарств от коронавируса до сих пор неверными.

In recent months, a social media post has circulated questioning the very existence of the coronavirus. The post claims that “no supermarket employee has been infected in the world,” suggesting that if the virus were real and as widespread as reported, supermarket workers—who have continued to interact with large numbers of people throughout the pandemic—would have been among the first to fall ill. This assertion has gained traction among those skeptical of COVID-19’s existence or severity. However, a closer look at the facts reveals significant inaccuracies and misleading conclusions.

To begin, it is important to understand the context of the coronavirus pandemic. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, emerged in late 2019 and quickly spread worldwide, leading to millions of confirmed cases and deaths. Essential workers, including supermarket employees, continued to operate during lockdowns, often with limited protective equipment in the early stages. Their exposure to customers placed them at heightened risk of contracting the virus.

The core claim of the social media post—that no supermarket employee has been infected anywhere in the world—does not hold up to scrutiny. Throughout the pandemic, numerous reports have surfaced of supermarket workers contracting COVID-19. Many supermarket chains across various countries have publicly acknowledged outbreaks among their staff, resulting in temporary store closures, sick leave, and even fatalities. News outlets have documented these cases, and supermarket companies themselves have implemented new safety measures such as mask mandates, plexiglass barriers, social distancing protocols, and vaccination drives specifically because their employees were at risk and, in many instances, had contracted the virus.

Furthermore, labor unions and advocacy groups have raised awareness about supermarket employees’ vulnerability to COVID-19. They have lobbied for hazard pay and improved safety standards, citing substantial numbers of infected workers. In some regions, supermarket employees were prioritized for early vaccination due to their exposure risk.

The post’s sweeping statement also ignores the global scale of the pandemic and the diversity of reporting practices. While some cases may not have been publicly disclosed or widely reported, there is overwhelming evidence that supermarket employees have not been immune. In fact, early in the pandemic, supermarkets were sites of concern for public health officials, who warned that crowded indoor environments could facilitate transmission.

The reasoning presented in the social media post demonstrates a misunderstanding of how infectious diseases spread and are documented. The absence of anecdotal evidence from a limited perspective does not equate to the absence of infections. Health authorities track cases using surveillance and reporting systems, not social media rumors or subjective observation. The sheer volume of infections across various professions, including supermarket workers, has been well established.

In summary, the claim that “no supermarket employee has been infected in the world” is demonstrably false. Supermarket workers have been affected by COVID-19 in significant numbers, prompting policy changes, public health interventions, and support measures. The existence of the coronavirus is well-documented, and the experience of supermarket employees underscores the reality of its impact. Assertions to the contrary misinform the public and risk undermining efforts to protect essential workers and the broader community.

အဆိုပါ အပတ်အတွင်း မိုဘိုင်းလ်ကို မျှဝေခဲ့သော ဆွေးနွေးမှုအရ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို တကယ်တမ်းမရှိသည်ဟု ဆိုလိုသည်။ အဆိုပါ ဆွေးနွေးမှုအရ ကမ္ဘာတစ်လွှဲမှုတွင် အမှားဖြစ်နေသည်ဟု ဆိုလိုသည်။ ကူးစက်ရောဂါက အမှန်တကယ် ကျွန်ုပ်တို့ ကြားသိရသည်အတိုင်း ပြန့်နှံ့နေသော်လည်း အမှုအရာကို ကူးစက်ရောဂါနှင့် ပတ်သက်၍ အကြီးအကျယ် လူအများကို ဆက်ဆံခဲ့သော ဆိုးရွားသော အလုပ်သမားများ အားလုံးသည် ပထမဆုံး နာလာခဲ့သည်ဟု ဆိုလိုသည်။ ထိုကဲ့သို့သော အဆိုပါ ဆွေးနွေးမှုများသည် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို တကယ်တမ်းမရှိသည် သို့မဟုတ် အလွန်ပြင်းထန်သည်ဟု အယူဝါဒအား တိုးတက်လာသည်။ သို့သော် အကြောင်းအရာကို အသေးစိတ် လေ့လာပါက အမှားကြီးများနှင့် မှားယွင်းသော အကဲဖြတ်မှုများ ရှိနေသည်ကို တွေ့ရပါမည်။

ပထမဦးစွာ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို လုပ်ဆောင်ရေးနှင့် ပတ်သက်၍ အကြောင်းအရာကို နားလည်သဘောပေါက်လိုက်ပါ။ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ဖြစ်ပေါ်စေသည့် SARS-CoV-2 ဗို့စ်ကို ၂၀၁၉ ခုနှစ် နောက်ပိုင်းတွင် ပေါ်ပေါက်ခဲ့ပြီး ကမ္ဘာအနှံ့သို့ ပျံ့နှံ့လာပြီး သန်းချိန်းကြိမ်များကို အတည်ပြုပြီး သေဆုံးမှုများကို ဖြစ်ပေါ်ခဲ့သည်။ အဓိကအလုပ်သမားများကို အိမ်နေချိန်များတွင် ဆက်လက် လုပ်ဆောင်ခဲ့ပြီး အစပိုင်းတွင် ကာကွယ်ရေးကိရိယာများကို အသုံးပြုခွင့်ရခြင်း မရှိသော်လည်း သူတို့သည် ဧည့်သည်များနှင့် ဆက်သွယ်ရေးကို အားကိုးခဲ့သည့်အတွက် ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ခံရန် ကျော်လွန်သော နေရာများတွင် တွေ့ရပါမည်။

အဆိုပါ မိုဘိုင်းလ်ကို မျှဝေခဲ့သော ဆွေးနွေးမှု၏ အဓိက အကြောင်းအရာမှာ ကမ္ဘာတစ်လွှဲမှုတွင် အမှားဖြစ်နေသည်ဟု ဆိုလိုသည်။ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို နောက်ဆုံးတွင် အမှားဖြစ်နေသည်ဟု ဆိုလိုသည်။ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို အကြောင်းအရာကို နားလည်သော အလုပ်သမားများအား အကြောင်းအရာကို ရှာဖွေရာတွင် များစွာ ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို ခံရသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို များစွာ တွေ့ရပါမည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို အများအပြား နိုင်ငံများတွင် အလုပ်သမားများအား ကူးစက်ရောဂါကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု သတင်းများက မှတ်တမ်းတင်ပြီး အလုပ်သမားများအား ကျော်လွန်ခဲ့သော ကြားပိုင်း နေရာများကို ပိတ်ပင်ခဲ့သည်၊ နာလာခဲ့သည် နှင့် အဆိုးရွားဆုံး အဆိုးရွားကို အမှီအခိုင်ကို ရရှိခဲ့သည်။ သတင်းထုတ်ပြန်ချက်များက အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို မှတ်တမ်းတင်ပြီး အလုပ်သမားများအား ပိုမို ကာကွယ်ရေးကိရိယာများကို ကျော်လွန်ခဲ့သည်။ ဥပမာ မျက်နှာပိုင်းကာကွယ်ရေးကိရိယာများ၊ သံပိုးကွက်များ၊ အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို ကျော်လွန်ခဲ့သည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို ပိုမို ကာကွယ်ရေးကိရိယာများကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို တွေ့ရပါမည်။

ပိုမိုအထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အဆိုပါ ဆွေးနွေးမှုက စွန့်ပစ်ခဲ့သည်။ ကမ္ဘာလေးတွင် အကြောင်းအရာကို နှိုင်းယှဉ်ပြီး အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို သာမန် တွေ့ရှိခဲ့သော်လည်း အကြောင်းအရာကို အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို အလွန်ပြင်းထန်သည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။ အကြောင်းအရာကို အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်ဟု အကြောင်းအရာကို အထူးပြုသည်။

A recent social media post claims, “In 2003, the global elite failed to run a PR campaign on coronavirus.” This statement suggests that a coordinated group of influential individuals or organizations—often referred to as the “global elite”—attempted, but failed, to manage public perception regarding a coronavirus outbreak in 2003. To assess this claim, it is important to examine the events surrounding the 2003 coronavirus epidemic, consider the role of public relations during that time, and analyze the concept of a coordinated elite campaign.

In 2003, the world experienced an outbreak of a novel coronavirus known as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS). SARS originated in southern China in late 2002 and quickly spread to several countries, including Canada, Singapore, and Vietnam, ultimately resulting in more than 8,000 cases and nearly 800 deaths worldwide. Unlike COVID-19, which emerged in 2019, SARS was contained relatively quickly after aggressive public health measures were implemented.

The public response to SARS in 2003 was marked by significant anxiety and intense media coverage, especially in affected regions. Governments and health organizations, including the World Health Organization (WHO), played central roles in disseminating information and coordinating health responses. The communication strategy focused on transparency, risk communication, and public guidance. There is no credible evidence that a group commonly referred to as the “global elite”—such as multinational corporate leaders, major political figures, or secretive organizations—attempted or orchestrated a global public relations (PR) campaign concerning the SARS coronavirus.

A recent social media post claims that “the chemtrails above Riga show that coronavirus is disseminated by the aircrafts.” This statement suggests that aircraft flying over Riga are intentionally releasing coronavirus into the atmosphere through so-called “chemtrails.” The post echoes longstanding conspiracy theories linking visible trails left by airplanes to secret government or organizational plots. In order to assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the science behind airplane contrails, the origins of the “chemtrail” conspiracy theory, and the known methods of coronavirus transmission.

To begin, the phenomenon of “chemtrails”—short for chemical trails—arose in the 1990s. The conspiracy theory alleges that the visible trails left behind by airplanes are not merely water vapor, but deliberate chemical or biological agents sprayed for various nefarious purposes. In reality, what people commonly see in the sky are contrails, short for “condensation trails.” These are formed when hot, humid air from jet exhaust mixes with the colder, low-pressure atmosphere at high altitudes, causing water vapor to condense and freeze into ice crystals. The resulting streaks can persist for minutes or hours, depending on atmospheric conditions. The process is well understood in meteorology and aviation, and there is no scientific evidence that these trails contain anything other than water vapor and trace exhaust gases.

The claim that coronavirus is being disseminated by aircraft through chemtrails lacks any scientific basis. Coronavirus, specifically SARS-CoV-2, is a respiratory virus that spreads primarily through person-to-person contact, respiratory droplets, and, to a lesser extent, airborne particles in enclosed spaces. There is no documented instance of a virus being dispersed via high-altitude aircraft in the manner described by the chemtrail conspiracy theory. Dispersion of viruses at such altitudes would not be an effective means of transmission, as the particles would be rapidly diluted and dispersed by atmospheric currents, and the survival of the virus in the harsh conditions of the upper atmosphere is highly unlikely.

Further, international aviation authorities, health agencies, and scientific experts have repeatedly stated that chemtrails are not real and that there are no programs to disseminate viruses or chemicals from commercial or military aircraft. The visual presence of contrails above Riga is a common occurrence in cities near major flight paths and does not correlate with disease outbreaks.

It is understandable that, during times of crisis such as the COVID-19 pandemic, misinformation and conspiracy theories can proliferate as people seek explanations for frightening events. However, attributing the spread of coronavirus to aircraft or chemtrails diverts attention from proven prevention measures such as vaccination, mask-wearing, and social distancing.

In summary, the assertion that coronavirus is being spread above Riga by aircraft through chemtrails is not supported by scientific evidence. The visible trails in the sky are a normal byproduct of aviation and contain no biological agents. The spread of coronavirus follows established patterns of human-to-human transmission, not aerial dispersal. It is vital to rely on verified information from scientific and health authorities when seeking to understand and combat public health threats.

In recent social media posts, Gemma O’Doherty, a former Irish journalist known for her controversial views, has claimed that state authorities in Ireland have confirmed that Covid-19 does not exist. This assertion has attracted significant attention online, with some users sharing the claim as evidence that the coronavirus pandemic is a hoax. However, a thorough review of available information reveals that this claim is false and misleading.

Gemma O’Doherty has been a vocal critic of government responses to the Covid-19 pandemic and has spread various conspiracy theories regarding the virus and public health measures. The specific claim that Irish state authorities have “confirmed” that Covid-19 does not exist appears to stem from a misinterpretation of official correspondence between O’Doherty and the Health Service Executive (HSE) of Ireland.

Background on the Claim

The origin of this claim traces back to a Freedom of Information (FOI) request made by O’Doherty or her associates, asking the HSE to provide proof of the isolation of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which causes Covid-19. In response, the HSE explained that while it does not hold physical samples of the virus within its administrative offices, the existence of the virus is well-established through scientific research and laboratory testing conducted globally and within Ireland. The response did not, at any point, state or suggest that Covid-19 does not exist.

Fact-Checking Analysis

The HSE, along with Ireland’s Department of Health and other scientific bodies, has consistently recognized the presence of Covid-19 in Ireland. Since the beginning of the pandemic, thousands of Covid-19 cases have been confirmed through laboratory testing, and the country has implemented widespread public health measures to contain outbreaks. Hospitals, healthcare providers, and scientific laboratories have reported and sequenced the virus, confirming its presence in the population.

The assertion that the authorities have “confirmed” the non-existence of Covid-19 misrepresents the facts. The original FOI response simply clarified the nature of the information held by the HSE and did not refute the existence of the virus. The scientific consensus, both in Ireland and internationally, is unequivocal: SARS-CoV-2 exists and causes Covid-19, which has led to millions of infections and deaths worldwide.

Context and Implications

Misinformation about the existence of Covid-19 undermines public health efforts and can fuel vaccine hesitancy and resistance to public health measures. The claim made by O’Doherty is part of a broader trend of conspiracy theories circulating online, often based on misunderstandings or deliberate misinterpretations of official documents.

In summary, the claim that Irish state authorities have confirmed that Covid-19 does not exist is false. No official body in Ireland has made such a statement. The HSE and other authorities continue to recognize the reality of Covid-19 and are actively engaged in managing its impact. It is important for the public to rely on credible, evidence-based sources when seeking information about the pandemic.

A recent social media post alleges that vaccination leads to infection and more severe illness, and further claims that vaccines are experimental and have not been properly tested. The statement is attributed to Alexander Redko, a doctor of medical sciences based in St. Petersburg. This article aims to examine the accuracy of these claims in the context of scientific consensus and available evidence.

The post centers on two core assertions: first, that vaccination causes individuals to become infected and experience more severe illness; second, that vaccines are experimental and have not undergone sufficient testing. Both claims have been widely circulated throughout the COVID-19 pandemic and during previous public health efforts involving mass vaccination.

To address the first claim, it is important to understand how vaccines work. Vaccines are designed to stimulate the immune system by introducing a harmless component of a pathogen, such as a protein or inactivated virus, prompting the body to develop immunity without causing the disease. There is no evidence that vaccines themselves cause infection with the disease they are intended to prevent. In rare cases, some live-attenuated vaccines can cause mild symptoms similar to the targeted illness, but these are generally far less severe than the natural infection and are a known and monitored part of vaccine safety profiles.

The assertion that vaccination leads to more severe illness is contradicted by extensive clinical and real-world data. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccinated individuals were consistently shown to be at significantly lower risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death compared to those who were unvaccinated. Breakthrough infections—cases where vaccinated individuals contract the illness—do occur, but the severity is typically much reduced. This pattern holds true for many other vaccines, such as those for influenza, measles, and hepatitis.

The second claim, that vaccines are experimental and have not been tested, is also misleading. Before approval for general use, vaccines undergo rigorous testing in multiple phases of clinical trials. These trials are designed to assess safety, efficacy, and potential side effects. Only after successful completion and regulatory review are vaccines authorized for widespread use. During the COVID-19 pandemic, vaccine development was expedited, but the fundamental steps of testing were maintained, with tens of thousands of participants enrolled in clinical trials before any vaccine was approved for emergency or regular use.

It is true that monitoring continues after approval, and rare side effects may be identified as millions of doses are administered. This ongoing process is standard for all medicines and vaccines, and is part of a robust safety system.

In summary, the claims made in the social media post attributed to Alexander Redko do not align with the established scientific evidence. Vaccines do not cause the illnesses they are designed to prevent, nor do they increase the severity of disease. The characterization of vaccines as untested or purely experimental ignores the extensive clinical trials and regulatory oversight involved in vaccine development. Misinformation of this kind can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and undermine public health efforts, highlighting the importance of relying on credible, evidence-based sources when discussing medical interventions.

article_content:
As COVID-19 vaccines have become a central tool in the fight against the pandemic, misinformation and concerns about their safety have circulated widely. A recent social media post claims that the spike protein produced by RNA (mRNA) vaccines is toxic and remains in the body for prolonged periods, causing harm. To address this claim, it is important to examine how mRNA vaccines work, what scientific evidence shows about the spike protein, and whether the concerns raised are supported by current research.

Understanding mRNA Vaccines and the Spike Protein

The Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines, both mRNA vaccines, use a small piece of genetic code (messenger RNA) to instruct cells to produce the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. This spike protein is not the virus itself but a harmless fragment designed to trigger an immune response. The body recognizes the protein as foreign, mounts an immune reaction, and develops defenses that protect against future infection.

The mRNA in the vaccine is encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles, allowing it to enter cells. Once inside, cells use the instructions to make the spike protein, display it on their surface, and then the mRNA is rapidly broken down by normal cellular processes. The spike protein is also temporary; the body’s immune system quickly identifies and eliminates it, and the cells that produced it.

Analyzing the Claim of Toxicity

The claim that the spike protein is inherently toxic and harmful is not supported by the bulk of scientific evidence. The spike protein produced by the vaccine is similar to that found on the actual virus but is present in much smaller quantities and for a much shorter duration. Studies have shown that the immune system clears the protein soon after vaccination. Furthermore, clinical trials and real-world monitoring of millions of vaccinated individuals have found no evidence that the spike protein produced by the vaccines causes widespread toxicity or harm.

It is important to distinguish between the spike protein as part of the intact SARS-CoV-2 virus and the isolated spike protein generated by the vaccine. In the context of infection, the virus’s spike protein aids in cell entry and is associated with the virus’s pathogenic effects. However, the vaccine-induced spike protein does not have the ability to replicate or cause infection. The immune response it stimulates is controlled and does not result in the same disease process as the virus itself.

Persistence in the Body

Another concern raised is that the spike protein “stays in the organism” for an extended period. Available research indicates that both the mRNA from the vaccine and the spike protein are quickly degraded and eliminated from the body. The mRNA breaks down within hours to a few days, and the spike protein is removed by the immune system shortly thereafter. There is no credible evidence to suggest that the spike protein persists long-term or accumulates in organs as a result of vaccination.

Conclusion

The claim that the spike protein produced by mRNA vaccines is toxic and remains in the body is not supported by scientific evidence. The protein is produced temporarily, is not inherently toxic in the context of vaccination, and is quickly cleared by the immune system. mRNA vaccines have undergone rigorous safety testing and real-world monitoring, demonstrating their safety and effectiveness in preventing COVID-19. As with any medical intervention, ongoing research continues to monitor for rare side effects, but the core claim presented in the social media post is not substantiated by current scientific understanding.

மாற்றியமைக்கப்பட்ட RNA மருந்துகளும் சிப்பாதியின் புலமும்

பிஎஃப்சிர்-பியோஎன்டெக் மற்றும் மாடர்னா கொரோனா வைரஸ் மருந்துகள் இரண்டும் மாற்றியமைக்கப்பட்ட RNA (mRNA) மருந்துகள் ஆகும். இவை உடலின் செல்களுக்கு தொடர்பு கொண்டு கொரோனா வைரஸின் சிப்பாதியின் புலம் உற்பத்தி செய்யும் தகவல் குறிப்பு (messenger RNA) கொண்டு மட்டுமே இருக்கின்றன. இந்த சிப்பாதியின் புலம் வைரஸின் முழு உடல் அல்ல, பாதுகாப்பான ஒரு துண்டு ஆகும், இது ஒரு இரசாயன பதிலைத் தூண்டும். உடல் அந்த புலத்தை வெளிப்படுத்தும் புறப்பட்டு, வைரஸின் எதிர்ப்பு தூண்டுவதும் இருக்கின்றது.

மருந்தில் உள்ள mRNA மெல்லிய நானோ துவர்களில் பாதுகாக்கப்பட்டுள்ளது, இதனால் செல்களில் பெருமளவில் செல்ல முடியும். செல்லினுள் பெருமளவில் இருந்து, சிப்பாதியின் புலம் உற்பத்தி செய்யப்படுகின்றது, அதை செல்லின் முன் பக்கத்தில் காட்டுவதும் மற்றும் பின்னர் mRNA கோளாறுகள் மூலம் உடலின் இயற்கை பெருமளவில் அழிக்கப்படுகின்றது. சிப்பாதியின் புலம் தொடர்புடையதும் அதை உடலின் இயற்கை எதிர்ப்பு முறைகளால் உடனடியாக அழிக்கப்படுகின்றது மற்றும் அது உற்பத்தி செய்த செல்களும் அழிக்கப்படுகின்றன.

மருந்துகளால் உருவாக்கப்படும் சிப்பாதியின் புலம் மூலம் தீங்கு விளைவிக்கும் என்ற கூற்று பெரும்பாலான விஞ்ஞான ஆதாரங்களால் ஆதரிக்கப்படவில்லை. மருந்துகளால் உருவாக்கப்படும் சிப்பாதியின் புலம் உண்மையான வைரஸில் காணப்படும் புலம் போல் இருக்கின்றது, ஆனால் அது குறைந்த அளவில் மற்றும் குறைந்த காலம் இருக்கின்றது. ஆராய்ச்சிகள் காட்டுகின்றன மருத்துவ சோதனைகள் மற்றும் மில்லியன்கள் மருத்துவமனைகளில் காணப்படும் மருந்து பெற்றவர்களின் விசாரணைகள் மருந்துகளால் உருவாக்கப்படும் சிப்பாதியின் புலம் விரிசலின் பெருமளவில் தீங்கு விளைவிக்காது அல்லது காயம் உண்டாக்காது என்பதை காட்டுகின்றன.

A recent social media post has gone viral, claiming, “Vaccinated people will never be able to donate blood.” This statement has caused confusion and concern among many, particularly as blood donation remains a vital part of healthcare systems worldwide. To assess the veracity of this claim, it’s important to examine current medical guidelines, the science behind blood donation, and the impact of vaccination on donor eligibility.

The claim appears to suggest that those who have received any vaccine—such as those for COVID-19, influenza, or other common diseases—are permanently disqualified from ever donating blood. This assertion is not supported by any major health authority or blood donation organization. In fact, the vast majority of vaccines, including those developed for COVID-19, do not exclude individuals from donating blood either temporarily or permanently.

Blood donation organizations routinely update their eligibility criteria based on the latest scientific evidence and guidance from health authorities. For most vaccines, such as those for measles, mumps, rubella, or seasonal flu, no deferral period is required, meaning individuals can donate blood immediately after vaccination, provided they are feeling well. In the case of the COVID-19 vaccines, guidelines have generally stated that people can donate blood as long as they are symptom-free and feel healthy. Some organizations may recommend waiting for a short period, typically 48 hours, after receiving certain types of vaccines to ensure there are no side effects like fever, but this is a precautionary measure rather than a restriction.

The rationale behind any temporary deferral is to protect both the donor and the recipient. For example, if a donor experiences side effects such as fever or malaise after vaccination, they may be deferred until they recover to ensure that the donation process is safe for everyone involved. However, these recommendations are temporary and do not constitute a permanent ban.

It is important to recognize that millions of people around the world have received vaccines, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Blood shortages remain a concern, and blood donation organizations continue to encourage eligible individuals—including those who have been vaccinated—to donate blood.

In summary, the claim that “Vaccinated people will never be able to donate blood” is false. Vaccinated individuals are generally eligible to donate blood, with only minor and temporary restrictions that may apply depending on the vaccine received and the donor’s health status at the time of donation. Spreading misinformation about blood donation eligibility can discourage potential donors and exacerbate blood shortages, potentially putting patients at risk. It is always advisable to consult official blood donation guidelines or contact local blood donation centers for the most up-to-date information.

In recent years, public discussions around COVID-19 vaccines have been marked by a proliferation of claims and counterclaims on social media. A viral post states: “Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla could not go visit Israel since he has not been vaccinated and that's all you should know about the vaccines.” This post implies that the head of one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies, responsible for developing a leading COVID-19 vaccine, has not been vaccinated himself. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the circumstances of Albert Bourla’s travel plans, his vaccination status, and the broader context.

Albert Bourla, as CEO of Pfizer, has been at the forefront of the company’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Pfizer’s vaccine, developed in partnership with BioNTech, was one of the first authorized for emergency use in several countries and has played a significant role in global vaccination efforts. The suggestion that Bourla himself was unvaccinated quickly drew attention and speculation.

The origin of the claim traces back to an incident in March 2021. Bourla was scheduled to visit Israel, a country that led the world in early vaccine rollout, to meet with officials and discuss vaccine supply. Reports emerged that his trip had been postponed. Some outlets and social media users speculated that Bourla was unable to travel because he had not yet been vaccinated, inferring reluctance or hypocrisy.

However, the facts reveal a different story. Bourla stated publicly that he had not yet received the vaccine at the time because he was not eligible under the prioritization guidelines in the United States, which initially reserved doses for healthcare workers, the elderly, and high-risk groups. Bourla, born in 1961, did not qualify as a frontline worker or an elderly individual during the initial phase of vaccine distribution. He also expressed his intention to wait his turn, adhering to public health recommendations rather than seeking preferential treatment.

Later, Bourla confirmed that he had received the vaccine when he became eligible. The suggestion that he remained unvaccinated is therefore inaccurate. The postponement of his Israel trip coincided with both the vaccination rollout schedule and potential travel restrictions, but was not due to vaccine hesitancy or refusal.

The social media post’s implication that Bourla’s vaccination status should be a decisive factor in evaluating vaccine safety or efficacy is misleading. Vaccine hesitancy among public figures has been a subject of scrutiny, but in this case, Bourla’s actions were consistent with public health guidance. Furthermore, the safety and effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines have been evaluated by national and international health authorities, not solely by the personal choices of individual executives.

In summary, the claim that Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla could not visit Israel because he was unvaccinated distorts the facts. Bourla was not initially vaccinated due to eligibility rules, not personal opposition to vaccination. He subsequently received the vaccine when appropriate. The post’s broader insinuation about vaccine credibility lacks foundation and misrepresents both Bourla’s actions and the wider context of vaccine rollout.

Kjo postim implicon se kryetari i njëra nga të mëdhenjët kompani farmaceutike botërore, i cili është i përgjegjshëm për zhvillimin e një vakcine të njëjtës koronavirusi, nuk është vakcinuar vetë. Për të shqyrtuar saktësinë e kësaj pohimi, është e rëndësishme të përqendrohemi në rrethanat e planifikimit të lëvizjes së Bourlait, statusin e tij të vakcinimit dhe kontekstin e gjerë.

Albert Bourla, si CEO i Pfizerit, ka qënë në mesin e përgjegjësive të kompanisë në përgjegjësi ndaj pandemisë së koronavirusit. Vakcina e Pfizerit, zhvilluar në bashkëpunim me BioNTech, ishte një nga të parat që u lejuan përdorimi urgjent në disa vendet dhe ka luajtur një rol të rëndësishëm në përpunimet globale të vakcinimit. Pohimi se Bourla nuk është vakcinuar ka shkaktuar shpejt shqyrtim dhe spekulime.

Origjina e kësaj pohimi shkaktohet nga një incident në mars 2021. Bourla ishte programuar të shkoi në Izrael, vend që kishte liderë në shpërndarjen e hershme të vakcinës, për të ndërprerë me qeveritë dhe të diskutuar ofertën e vakcinës. Raportet janë shfaqur se lëvizja e tij ishte ndërprethet. Disa media dhe përdhënerët në media sociale kanë spekuluar se Bourla nuk mund të lëvizë sepse nuk ishte vakcinuar ende, duke inferuar rezistencë ose hipokrizi.

Por fakta tregojnë një histori të ndryshme. Bourla ka thënë publikisht se nuk ishte marrë vakcinën në kohën e tij sepse nuk ishte i përshtatshëm nën rregullat e prioritetit në Shtetet e Bashkuara, që në fillim kishin rezervuar doset për punëtorët e shërbimeve të shëndetësisë, të moshës së lartë dhe grupeve të rrezikshme. Bourla, i lindur në 1961, nuk ishte i përshtatshëm si punëtorë të parë ose person i moshës së lartë gjatë fazës së parë të shpërndarjes së vakcinës. Ai ka shprehur që do të pritë në rradhë, duke përballuar rekomandimet e shëndetësisë publike në vend që të kërkojë traktim të preferuar.

Më pas, Bourla ka konfirmuar se ai është marrë vakcinën në momentin kur ishte i përshtatshëm. Pohimi se ai është mbetur i pavakcinuar është, prandaj, i pavërtetë. Ndërpreja e lëvizjes së tij në Izrael ka përmbajtë të gjitha kohëzën e shpërndarjes së vakcinës dhe mundësive të ndërprejes së lëvizjes, por nuk ka qenë për shkak të rezistencës ose refuzimit të vakcinimit.

Pohimi në postimin e media sociale se statusi i vakcinimit të Bourlait duhet të jetë faktori i përgjithshëm në vlerësimin e sigurisë ose efikasitetit të vakcinës është i pavërtetë. Rrezistencja ndaj vakcinës në figurat publike ka qenë subjekt i shqyrtimit, por në këtë rast, veprimet e Bourlait janë qenë të përshtatshme me rekomandimet e shëndetësisë publike. Megjithatë, siguria dhe efikasiteti i vakcinës së koronavirusit janë vlerësuar nga autoritetet e shëndetësisë së vendit dhe botërore, jo vetëm nga zgjedhjet personale të ekzekutivëve të individëve.
